The sky is blue because of **Rayleigh scattering**. Sunlight contains many visible wavelengths. As it passes through the atmosphere, tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen scatter shorter wavelengths more strongly than longer wavelengths. The scattering strength is roughly proportional to `1 / wavelength^4`, so blue and violet light are redirected around the sky much more than red light.

Why not violet? Three main reasons combine. First, the Sun emits less violet than blue. Second, the upper atmosphere absorbs some ultraviolet and violet. Third, human eyes are not equally sensitive to all colors: our cone responses make the mixture of scattered short wavelengths look blue rather than violet. The perceived color is not just the strongest physical scattering wavelength; it is the spectrum after solar emission, atmospheric filtering, and human vision.

This also explains red sunsets. When the Sun is low, light travels through much more atmosphere. Much of the blue light is scattered out of the direct path before it reaches your eyes, leaving the direct solar disk and nearby clouds enriched in reds and oranges.

A related everyday phenomenon is the bluish haze of distant mountains. Air scatters short-wavelength light between you and the mountains, adding a blue veil. Similarly, smoke or milk diluted in water can look bluish from the side because small particles scatter shorter wavelengths preferentially.
